To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) tissue homing of human mesenchyma stem cells (MSC) in xenogeneic mice can be increased by CXCR4 overexpression; (2) tissue homing is diminished by prolonged culture of MSC in vitro; (3) tissue homing in young mice is greater than in adult mice; and (4) tissue homing can be enhanced by CXCR4 expression in irradiated hosts.

the homing of systematically infused mesenchymale stem cells to bone marrow and splenic tissues of unconditioned animals was significantly higher in younger animals and reduced with increasing passage of mesenchymale stromal cells.
the tissue homing of human mesenchym al stem cells in a β2m/Nod/Scid animal model can be increased by CXCR4 overexpression, at least in animals that had received a lethal dose of irradiation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of mesenchymale stem cells (MSCs) in tissue regeneration, enhancing haemopoietic stem cells transplantation and delivering genes for therapy
the use of human bone marrow mesenchymal cells (MSC) in regenerative medicine, and the development of gene transfer strategies using these cells as a vehicle for gene therapy.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the tissue homing of bone marrow derived mesenchymal cells can be influenced by several factors, including host age, in vitro expansion, and enforced over-expression of CXR4.
the tissue distribution of mesenchymnal stem cells is influenced both by host and cell factors.
tissue homing can be increased by CXCR4 over expression, but this is dependent on the irradiated host and not in unconditioned hosts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tissue homing and engraftment of human bone marrow derived mesenchymal cells can be increased in irradiated hosts by enforced expression of the chemokine receptor CXCR4.
mesenchymal cells home to sites of tissue injury, but this is influenced by the host environment.
the homing of systemcally injected mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) to the bone marrow of immunodeficient mice is significantly higher in younger animals, and reduced with increasing passage numbers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
tissue homing is not a passive process, but is influenced by a number of factors.

the tissue distribution of mesenchym al stem cells can be manipulated, and that this may be important in the development of strategies to enhance tissue regeneration or to deliver genes of therapeutic interest.
the age of the host animal and the duration of ex vivo culture of mesenchymall stem cells are important considerations for the design of clinical trials using these cells.
